compare_blocks.title: One-minute comparison

compare_blocks.body:
In the fictional inspection, either person can focus on the parts and the colour difference they see. The resemblance comes from the shared S — sourcing from observable facts and past experience rather than an abstract model as the main material. Conversely, no single workplace action can verify four letters: being conscientious, careful or able to carry a load all depend on the post, the shift and the scope of responsibility.

The difference sits on three preferences, read separately. ESTJ's attention turns outward more often, onto tasks, people and deliverable results; ISFP's turns inward more often, onto their own reactions and what they care about. In judging, ESTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently, and ISFP more often brings people, values and feelings into the weighing. In outer work, ESTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion, and ISFP more often keeps options and keeps taking in new information. The three are independent; one cannot be inferred from another.

### One batch with colour variance, two reasons for handling it

In this fictional inspection, both people have the same batch, authority, deadline and records. Either could check the sampling plan and consider how the parts look in use. The difference is which kind of basis becomes the main reason for the decision, and what gets cited under challenge.

One emphasis makes the decision reviewable: which version of the sampling plan applies, whether the limit sample carries both signatures, how a similar batch was handled last time. The other emphasis looks at the actual effect: two parts side by side at the window, turned at another angle, then fitted to a unit and viewed from a normal distance to see whether the difference is noticeable. Both costs are real: the first may reject a difference the user could never see; the second may leave no reproducible condition and be asked by the supplier "on what basis".

On one incoming inspection, forty of the sampled housings were noticeably yellow. The lot size and sample size are recorded per that batch's sampling plan; that number alone cannot decide whether the whole lot should be accepted. Whether a single part fails on colour is compared under the agreed light source, viewing distance and limit sample; whether the lot is accepted follows the applicable sampling plan and acceptance rules; how it looks on the assembled unit is recorded separately, and any concession is approved through the process. Keeping those three apart is more useful than arguing about who looked more carefully.

Two things count as evidence: whether the decision conditions can be reproduced by someone else (light source, angle, sample number written down), and whether a concession went through approval. What does not count is who looked more carefully, nor the order of actions. Keep the counterexamples: ESTJ will lean over the inspection bench for a long while on a disputed batch, and ISFP will check a sampling table line by line when signing a release.

### Why Te and Fi are shared while their positions swap end to end

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Only Te and Fi appear in both, and they swap first and last: ESTJ has Te first and Fi fourth, ISFP the reverse.

A position describes processing emphasis in this model; it does not say what someone thinks of first when deciding, and does not say who considers value or efficiency less. ESTJ's first position faces outward, putting attention more often on checkable results and assignable responsibility; ISFP's first faces inward, more often confirming first whether this is consistent with what they care about. The perceiving side changes entirely: Si and Ne on one side, referring to past experience and possibility; Se and Ni on the other, referring to the present concrete impression and what it implies. The two share the S letter but do not use the same Sensing process.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is disputed across sources: some mark an attitude for ESTJ's Ne and ISFP's Ni, others list only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone moves. compare_blocks.title: Why they are easily confused

compare_blocks.body:
What follows is the same batch of colour-variant parts, from decision to communication, and then one choice of colour in ordinary life. Scope note: the division follows authority, experience and familiarity with the evidence, not type; the final handling is signed off through the existing approval process, and disagreement stays in the record.

### After the colour decision, who talks to the supplier

(Fictional scene.) Once the decision is set, the supplier has to be faced. The division turns on three things: who has authority for outward communication, who knows this batch's sampling and assembly verification, and who holds the complete record. The lead negotiator brings the sampling record, the signed limit-sample page and the rework quotation, and states the return quantity and deadline; whoever knows the assembly verification arranges the comparison photographs by batch and points out which batch is most conspicuous on the finished unit. Missing either set of material gets the negotiation pushed back.

The constraint is that the supplier looks only at evidence, not at adjectives. With the tables complete but no photographs, the reply is "no visible difference"; with persuasive photographs but no numbers or light source noted, the reply is "it looks different under another lamp".

A workable verification step: for each disputed batch keep one three-cell card — light source and angle, sample number, decision-maker. That is the minimum record for review; it does not guarantee that everyone reaches the same conclusion, but with the conditions written down the disagreement at least sits on the same facts.

### Helping a friend choose a sign for a small noodle shop

(Fictional scene.) A friend is opening a shop and asks both to help decide the sign. Either may first ask whether the local authority requires registration, what size limit applies and how long fabrication takes; either may first look at how the lettering reads under evening light and whether the background clashes with the two shops next door. The more usual division has each watching the end they care about more: one fears the sign being taken down and the money wasted, the other fears a sign that is lit but draws nobody in.

This is not about who understands aesthetics better, or who is more rule-abiding. A workable approach does both: whoever knows the process handles registration and lead time, whoever is more sensitive to the effect sets the colours and the typeface, and before submission both stand across the road at dusk and look once. One counterexample on each side: ESTJ will go three rounds with the fabricator over the spacing of one character; ISFP will go and check the registration requirements unprompted.

### The supplier arrives with their own colour chips for a recheck

(Fictional scene.) Their quality manager argues there is no difference between the two batches under the standard light source. Either may put the signed limit sample on the table and ask whether it is still valid; either may fit one part from each batch to a unit, wheel it to the doorway in natural light and let the other side look. The more common difference: one pulls the discussion back to the contract and the criterion, the other back to the effect actually seen.

The condition for changing the order is not in a type but in the contract: if it specifies the judging light source and the sample, discuss the basis first; if it does not, looking at the parts first reaches agreement more easily, then a conditions annex is added. Either person could overlook the addendum. If the agreed conditions are not recorded, the next batch may raise the same question.
compare_blocks.title: Illustrative scenarios

compare_blocks.body:
Following an agreed acceptance rule does not show that someone is indifferent to the supplier. Either type can follow the procedure and explain the decision clearly.

The second trap is reading "goes by feel" as unprofessional. An observation that the colour looks different can be a starting point for a documented check under the agreed conditions. It does not tell you which checks have already been done or what the observer’s type is.

The third trap is tidiness and craft. A neat workstation with tools lined up has nothing to do with type; making something that feels right in the hand has nothing to do with type either. Still less should anyone infer who is better suited to inspection or to design — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.

The fourth trap is treating the shared S as "tougher, more down to earth". Sensing describes a sourcing preference only; whether someone can handle night shifts depends on physical capacity, the shift arrangement and their family situation.

The fifth trap is using the order of actions as a criterion. Who opens the file first and who picks up the part first depends on authority, deadline and who is present, and the same type may reverse it on another shift.

body: In the fictional inspection, either person can focus on the parts and the colour difference they see. The resemblance comes from the shared S — sourcing from observable facts and past experience rather than an abstract model as the main material. Conversely, no single workplace action can verify four letters: being conscientious, careful or able to carry a load all depend on the post, the shift and the scope of responsibility.

The difference sits on three preferences, read separately. ESTJ's attention turns outward more often, onto tasks, people and deliverable results; ISFP's turns inward more often, onto their own reactions and what they care about. In judging, ESTJ more often relies on impersonal criteria that can be applied consistently, and ISFP more often brings people, values and feelings into the weighing. In outer work, ESTJ more often forms an arrangement and a conclusion, and ISFP more often keeps options and keeps taking in new information. The three are independent; one cannot be inferred from another.
### One batch with colour variance, two reasons for handling it

In this fictional inspection, both people have the same batch, authority, deadline and records. Either could check the sampling plan and consider how the parts look in use. The difference is which kind of basis becomes the main reason for the decision, and what gets cited under challenge.

One emphasis makes the decision reviewable: which version of the sampling plan applies, whether the limit sample carries both signatures, how a similar batch was handled last time. The other emphasis looks at the actual effect: two parts side by side at the window, turned at another angle, then fitted to a unit and viewed from a normal distance to see whether the difference is noticeable. Both costs are real: the first may reject a difference the user could never see; the second may leave no reproducible condition and be asked by the supplier "on what basis".

On one incoming inspection, forty of the sampled housings were noticeably yellow. The lot size and sample size are recorded per that batch's sampling plan; that number alone cannot decide whether the whole lot should be accepted. Whether a single part fails on colour is compared under the agreed light source, viewing distance and limit sample; whether the lot is accepted follows the applicable sampling plan and acceptance rules; how it looks on the assembled unit is recorded separately, and any concession is approved through the process. Keeping those three apart is more useful than arguing about who looked more carefully.

Two things count as evidence: whether the decision conditions can be reproduced by someone else (light source, angle, sample number written down), and whether a concession went through approval. What does not count is who looked more carefully, nor the order of actions. Keep the counterexamples: ESTJ will lean over the inspection bench for a long while on a disputed batch, and ISFP will check a sampling table line by line when signing a release.
### Why Te and Fi are shared while their positions swap end to end

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Only Te and Fi appear in both, and they swap first and last: ESTJ has Te first and Fi fourth, ISFP the reverse.

A position describes processing emphasis in this model; it does not say what someone thinks of first when deciding, and does not say who considers value or efficiency less. ESTJ's first position faces outward, putting attention more often on checkable results and assignable responsibility; ISFP's first faces inward, more often confirming first whether this is consistent with what they care about. The perceiving side changes entirely: Si and Ne on one side, referring to past experience and possibility; Se and Ni on the other, referring to the present concrete impression and what it implies. The two share the S letter but do not use the same Sensing process.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is disputed across sources: some mark an attitude for ESTJ's Ne and ISFP's Ni, others list only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone moves. Base preferences are in the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).

body: What follows is the same batch of colour-variant parts, from decision to communication, and then one choice of colour in ordinary life. Scope note: the division follows authority, experience and familiarity with the evidence, not type; the final handling is signed off through the existing approval process, and disagreement stays in the record.
### After the colour decision, who talks to the supplier

(Fictional scene.) Once the decision is set, the supplier has to be faced. The division turns on three things: who has authority for outward communication, who knows this batch's sampling and assembly verification, and who holds the complete record. The lead negotiator brings the sampling record, the signed limit-sample page and the rework quotation, and states the return quantity and deadline; whoever knows the assembly verification arranges the comparison photographs by batch and points out which batch is most conspicuous on the finished unit. Missing either set of material gets the negotiation pushed back.

The constraint is that the supplier looks only at evidence, not at adjectives. With the tables complete but no photographs, the reply is "no visible difference"; with persuasive photographs but no numbers or light source noted, the reply is "it looks different under another lamp".

A workable verification step: for each disputed batch keep one three-cell card — light source and angle, sample number, decision-maker. That is the minimum record for review; it does not guarantee that everyone reaches the same conclusion, but with the conditions written down the disagreement at least sits on the same facts.
### Helping a friend choose a sign for a small noodle shop

(Fictional scene.) A friend is opening a shop and asks both to help decide the sign. Either may first ask whether the local authority requires registration, what size limit applies and how long fabrication takes; either may first look at how the lettering reads under evening light and whether the background clashes with the two shops next door. The more usual division has each watching the end they care about more: one fears the sign being taken down and the money wasted, the other fears a sign that is lit but draws nobody in.

This is not about who understands aesthetics better, or who is more rule-abiding. A workable approach does both: whoever knows the process handles registration and lead time, whoever is more sensitive to the effect sets the colours and the typeface, and before submission both stand across the road at dusk and look once. One counterexample on each side: ESTJ will go three rounds with the fabricator over the spacing of one character; ISFP will go and check the registration requirements unprompted.
### The supplier arrives with their own colour chips for a recheck

(Fictional scene.) Their quality manager argues there is no difference between the two batches under the standard light source. Either may put the signed limit sample on the table and ask whether it is still valid; either may fit one part from each batch to a unit, wheel it to the doorway in natural light and let the other side look. The more common difference: one pulls the discussion back to the contract and the criterion, the other back to the effect actually seen.

The condition for changing the order is not in a type but in the contract: if it specifies the judging light source and the sample, discuss the basis first; if it does not, looking at the parts first reaches agreement more easily, then a conditions annex is added. Either person could overlook the addendum. If the agreed conditions are not recorded, the next batch may raise the same question.

body: Following an agreed acceptance rule does not show that someone is indifferent to the supplier. Either type can follow the procedure and explain the decision clearly.

The second trap is reading "goes by feel" as unprofessional. An observation that the colour looks different can be a starting point for a documented check under the agreed conditions. It does not tell you which checks have already been done or what the observer’s type is.

The third trap is tidiness and craft. A neat workstation with tools lined up has nothing to do with type; making something that feels right in the hand has nothing to do with type either. Still less should anyone infer who is better suited to inspection or to design — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.

The fourth trap is treating the shared S as "tougher, more down to earth". Sensing describes a sourcing preference only; whether someone can handle night shifts depends on physical capacity, the shift arrangement and their family situation.

The fifth trap is using the order of actions as a criterion. Who opens the file first and who picks up the part first depends on authority, deadline and who is present, and the same type may reverse it on another shift.

One emphasis makes the decision reviewable: which version of the sampling plan applies, whether the limit sample carries both signatures, how a similar batch was handled last time. The other emphasis looks at the actual effect: two parts side by side at the window, turned at another angle, then fitted to a unit and viewed from a normal distance to see whether the difference is noticeable. Both costs are real: the first may reject a difference the user could never see; the second may leave no reproducible condition and be asked by the supplier "on what basis".

On one incoming inspection, forty of the sampled housings were noticeably yellow. The lot size and sample size are recorded per that batch's sampling plan; that number alone cannot decide whether the whole lot should be accepted. Whether a single part fails on colour is compared under the agreed light source, viewing distance and limit sample; whether the lot is accepted follows the applicable sampling plan and acceptance rules; how it looks on the assembled unit is recorded separately, and any concession is approved through the process. Keeping those three apart is more useful than arguing about who looked more carefully.

Two things count as evidence: whether the decision conditions can be reproduced by someone else (light source, angle, sample number written down), and whether a concession went through approval. What does not count is who looked more carefully, nor the order of actions. Keep the counterexamples: ESTJ will lean over the inspection bench for a long while on a disputed batch, and ISFP will check a sampling table line by line when signing a release.

### Why Te and Fi are shared while their positions swap end to end

In the common four-function notation used here, ESTJ is Te–Si–Ne–Fi and ISFP is Fi–Se–Ni–Te. Only Te and Fi appear in both, and they swap first and last: ESTJ has Te first and Fi fourth, ISFP the reverse.

A position describes processing emphasis in this model; it does not say what someone thinks of first when deciding, and does not say who considers value or efficiency less. ESTJ's first position faces outward, putting attention more often on checkable results and assignable responsibility; ISFP's first faces inward, more often confirming first whether this is consistent with what they care about. The perceiving side changes entirely: Si and Ne on one side, referring to past experience and possibility; Se and Ni on the other, referring to the present concrete impression and what it implies. The two share the S letter but do not use the same Sensing process.

Whether the third process is labelled introverted or extraverted is disputed across sources: some mark an attitude for ESTJ's Ne and ISFP's Ni, others list only the function name. The disagreement does not change the first two positions and does not explain how early anyone moves. Base preferences are in the [ESTJ profile](/en/personality/estj) and the [ISFP profile](/en/personality/isfp).

The premise is aligned conditions: the same batch with colour variance, the same sampling plan, the same limit sample, the same delivery date and authority. Either may check the procedure first, and either may look at the parts first; the table records only which kind of basis is used as the reason more often in the same scene.

| The same batch (one plan, one limit sample, the same date and authority) | ESTJ: the basis more likely attended to | ISFP: the basis more likely attended to | What this row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Whether this lot should be rejected | Apply the same verified acceptance rules and approved sample used for comparable lots | Weigh how the same confirmed variation would affect users once the parts are assembled | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |
| How a single part should be compared | Check the part under the agreed lighting and viewing conditions, using the approved reference sample | Use the same inspection conditions and document any separate observations about appearance in use | Shared S: direct observations from the same inspection. Appearance in use is a separate question. |
| The supplier asks "on what basis" | Use the same acceptance criteria to explain the decision from the verified sample and photos | Use the same verified sample and photos to explain how the variation affects the end user | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F; both are reviewable evidence |
| Whether to raise a concession | May settle on a provisional recommendation under the same approval requirements | May keep several options open while both wait for the same assembly test | Outward stance, leaning J/P |
| When discussion stalls | May clarify the same concerns through discussion with the group | May clarify the same concerns by reflecting privately before returning to the discussion | E/I: where attention goes while making sense of the same discussion. Either can check both concerns. |
| The review afterwards | Check whether similar lots were judged by the same basis | Weigh what the documented variation meant for users of the assembled unit | Basis for judgement, leaning T/F |

The differences in the table are not a scale of ability. An ISFP with ten years in inspection more often checks item by item against remembered criteria, and an ESTJ taking this kind of lot for the first time may only stand at the bench and look. The same person also changes approach with the scope of authority, delivery pressure and the information at hand, so these rows cannot be used to classify.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFP in one minute

sections.body_md:
What follows is the same batch of colour-variant parts, from decision to communication, and then one choice of colour in ordinary life. Scope note: the division follows authority, experience and familiarity with the evidence, not type; the final handling is signed off through the existing approval process, and disagreement stays in the record.

### After the colour decision, who talks to the supplier

(Fictional scene.) Once the decision is set, the supplier has to be faced. The division turns on three things: who has authority for outward communication, who knows this batch's sampling and assembly verification, and who holds the complete record. The lead negotiator brings the sampling record, the signed limit-sample page and the rework quotation, and states the return quantity and deadline; whoever knows the assembly verification arranges the comparison photographs by batch and points out which batch is most conspicuous on the finished unit. Missing either set of material gets the negotiation pushed back.

The constraint is that the supplier looks only at evidence, not at adjectives. With the tables complete but no photographs, the reply is "no visible difference"; with persuasive photographs but no numbers or light source noted, the reply is "it looks different under another lamp".

A workable verification step: for each disputed batch keep one three-cell card — light source and angle, sample number, decision-maker. That is the minimum record for review; it does not guarantee that everyone reaches the same conclusion, but with the conditions written down the disagreement at least sits on the same facts.

### Helping a friend choose a sign for a small noodle shop

(Fictional scene.) A friend is opening a shop and asks both to help decide the sign. Either may first ask whether the local authority requires registration, what size limit applies and how long fabrication takes; either may first look at how the lettering reads under evening light and whether the background clashes with the two shops next door. The more usual division has each watching the end they care about more: one fears the sign being taken down and the money wasted, the other fears a sign that is lit but draws nobody in.

This is not about who understands aesthetics better, or who is more rule-abiding. A workable approach does both: whoever knows the process handles registration and lead time, whoever is more sensitive to the effect sets the colours and the typeface, and before submission both stand across the road at dusk and look once. One counterexample on each side: ESTJ will go three rounds with the fabricator over the spacing of one character; ISFP will go and check the registration requirements unprompted.

### The supplier arrives with their own colour chips for a recheck

(Fictional scene.) Their quality manager argues there is no difference between the two batches under the standard light source. Either may put the signed limit sample on the table and ask whether it is still valid; either may fit one part from each batch to a unit, wheel it to the doorway in natural light and let the other side look. The more common difference: one pulls the discussion back to the contract and the criterion, the other back to the effect actually seen.

The condition for changing the order is not in a type but in the contract: if it specifies the judging light source and the sample, discuss the basis first; if it does not, looking at the parts first reaches agreement more easily, then a conditions annex is added. Either person could overlook the addendum. If the agreed conditions are not recorded, the next batch may raise the same question.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFP at work and in everyday collaboration

sections.body_md:
Following an agreed acceptance rule does not show that someone is indifferent to the supplier. Either type can follow the procedure and explain the decision clearly.

The second trap is reading "goes by feel" as unprofessional. An observation that the colour looks different can be a starting point for a documented check under the agreed conditions. It does not tell you which checks have already been done or what the observer’s type is.

The third trap is tidiness and craft. A neat workstation with tools lined up has nothing to do with type; making something that feels right in the hand has nothing to do with type either. Still less should anyone infer who is better suited to inspection or to design — that turns a preference into a rank of ability.

The fourth trap is treating the shared S as "tougher, more down to earth". Sensing describes a sourcing preference only; whether someone can handle night shifts depends on physical capacity, the shift arrangement and their family situation.

The fifth trap is using the order of actions as a criterion. Who opens the file first and who picks up the part first depends on authority, deadline and who is present, and the same type may reverse it on another shift.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFP: avoiding misreads

sections.body_md:
When two results differ, check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then the situation you answered from: were you signing a release, or giving advice; how much authority, time and information did you have. The person signing leans to procedure, the person advising speaks from impression — that is the situation pushing the answer, not a change of preference.

Put the practice across several comparable situations, with no threshold on occasions. Take a few recent parts or matters where something felt "not quite right but hard to name", and write three lines for each: which information you trusted (S/N), which standard you weighed it against (T/F), and whether you settled the handling or kept options (J/P). Add one more line: would you rather handle this with someone, or digest it alone first (E/I). Whatever recurs is worth discussing as your habit, but it is not a typing rule.

If you use both approaches often, both are within your range, and that cannot be used to infer that you sit near a score boundary. Behaviour cannot be read backwards into a score either: the same type makes different choices under different authority, deadlines and information. If the item bank reports dimension scores, look at which sits near the boundary; without dimension scores or scoring notes, make no boundary inference.
sections.title: ESTJ and ISFP: how to keep observing

items.answer:
Because both look solid, direct and specific about parts in concrete matters, and "solid" is the most visible layer.

The difference hides in the three preferences, not in how conscientious either is: both source practically, but one refers more to an established criterion and the other more to the conditions in front of them; in judging, one weighs a consistently applicable standard and the other weighs people and values; outward, one more often settles an arrangement and the other keeps options. The shared Sensing makes both hold onto detail, so one scene cannot separate them — review which kind of basis is cited more often across comparable situations.
items.question: They differ on three letters — why are they still confused?

items.answer:
Because the positions differ: ESTJ leads with Te and has Fi fourth, and ISFP is the exact reverse.

In this model, a position describes a theoretical emphasis; it does not say what someone thinks of first when deciding, and does not say who considers value or efficiency less. ESTJ's Te faces outward, more often turning matters into checkable results and assignable responsibility; ISFP's Fi faces inward, more often confirming first whether this is consistent with what they care about. The attitude of the third process is labelled differently across sources, so check whether a differing version states its source.
items.question: Both have Te and Fi — why does it not work out the same?

items.answer:
Yes. Once the procedure is accepted, it is held as a floor, and the signature is no looser than anyone's.

The difference is the reason: one holds to "this is the criterion both sides agreed, and anyone else would reach the same conclusion", the other to "this batch going out damages the reputation and wastes the assembly team's work". Different reasons, the same action. Who signs a release depends on authority and process, not on type.
items.question: Can ISFP also reject a batch under procedure?

items.answer:
ESTJ more often watches whether the decision is reproducible: are the conditions written, are the signatures complete, were similar lots judged the same way; ISFP more often watches the gap between the decision and how it actually looks: the standard is met, but is it still noticeable on the assembled unit.

Both are necessary and both can be learned. The inspection record can be split into two columns, one for the decision basis and one for the actual appearance, with who owns which column agreed in advance. That is an arrangement of work, not a claim that one type can only do one column.
items.question: In an inspection post, what does each watch?

items.answer:
Most often "isn't that obvious": one means "it is already outside the standard", the other means "you cannot see it once it is assembled".

A workable move is to write both sentences into the record, then let the existing approval process decide who holds final authority; whoever holds it carries this release or rejection on the sign-off, and the other's opinion stays in the notes. Authority comes from delegation, not from type, and not from who cares more.
items.question: Working together, which sentence starts the argument?

items.answer:
Check the assessment name, version, language and scoring convention first, then the situation you were in and the kind of experience you referred to.

Then look separately at the three differing preferences: external interaction or inner reflection (E/I), consistent criteria or people and values in decisions (T/F), and settling an outward arrangement or keeping options open (J/P). S is shared. Record how duty, authority and time pressure changed your choices; what is being read is a long-term preference across situations, with no set number of observations. If the item bank gives no dimension scores or scoring notes, do not infer a boundary from behaviour.
